title: Strict Type Coercion Formatter
problemStatement: Implement `safeCast(value, targetType)` that explicitly and safely converts `value` to `'string'`, `'number'`, or `'boolean'`. For `'number'`, if conversion results in NaN, return `0` instead.
interviewTrap: Using `+value` or `parseInt` can cause subtle NaN or radix bugs. `Number(value)` with `Number.isNaN()` check is standard.

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: The engine coerces primitives via internal algorithms. In loose equality (`==`), boolean values are first coerced to numbers, objects are coerced via `ToPrimitive(hint)`, and `null == undefined` is exclusively true.
stepByStepWalkthrough: 1. Initialize execution context and environment records for Explicit Type Conversions & Truthiness.
2. Execute logic adhering to ECMAScript standard specification.
3. Verify invariant boundaries and edge conditions.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In JavaScript engines (e.g. V8), Explicit Type Conversions & Truthiness is optimized via inline caches, heap contexts, and bytecode translation.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: What is the difference between explicit conversion and implicit coercion?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: Explicit conversion occurs when a developer deliberately calls a constructor function without `new` to convert types (e.g. `Number('42')`, `Boolean(x)`, `String(123)`). Implicit coercion occurs automatically when operators (`+`, `-`, `==`, `if(x)`) force operands into different types according to ECMAScript coercion rules.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: Why does [] + [] evaluate to '' while [] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: The `+` operator triggers `ToPrimitive` on both operands. For arrays, `ToPrimitive` calls `toString()`, which produces an empty string `''`. Therefore `'' + '' === ''`. For `{}`, its `toString()` returns `'[object Object]'`, so `'' + '[object Object]' === '[object Object]'`.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Classic JS trivia that tests ToPrimitive algorithm knowledge.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: What are the exact falsy values in JavaScript?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: There are exactly 8 falsy values in modern ECMAScript: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n` (BigInt zero), `''` (empty string), `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN`. All other values (including `[]`, `{}`, `'0'`, and `'false'`) are strictly truthy.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Every developer must know the complete falsy list.

realWorldUseCases.description: HTML `<input>` values are always strings. Converting form state to typed payloads requires explicit numeric/boolean conversions.

realWorldUseCases.scenario: Boolean Flag Normalization in Environment Variables
realWorldUseCases.description: Reading `process.env.ENABLE_FEATURE`: strings like `'true'`, `'1'` must be normalized explicitly rather than relying on `Boolean(process.env.VAR)` (which evaluates `'false'` to `true`!).

howToExplain.opening: Type coercion in JavaScript is governed by formal abstract operations defined in ECMA-262: ToBoolean, ToNumber, ToString, and ToPrimitive.
keyPoints: Explicit conversion (Number(), Boolean(), String()) is clear, predictable, and maintainable.
Implicit coercion occurs automatically during binary operations and loose equality.
There are exactly 8 falsy values in JavaScript; all objects and arrays are truthy.
Always prefer explicit conversions to prevent subtle production bugs.
howToExplain.closingImpression: Coercion is not random magic; it follows strict mathematical rules laid out in the ECMAScript specification.
analogies: Like currency exchange: explicit conversion is going to an exchange booth; implicit coercion is the store automatically converting your foreign cash at the register with hidden fees.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using Boolean('false') expecting it to be false.
commonMistakes.why: Any non-empty string in JavaScript is truthy. Boolean('false') evaluates to true!

followUpDeepDive.question: Why does document.all evaluate as falsy in browsers despite being an object?
followUpDeepDive.answer: For web compatibility (Annex B.3.7), `document.all` has an exotic internal `[[IsHTMLDDA]]` slot that forces `ToBoolean(document.all)` to evaluate to `false` and `typeof document.all === 'undefined'`, allowing legacy code detecting IE to branch correctly while still allowing property access.
followUpDeepDive.specReference: ECMA-262 Annex B.3.7 The [[IsHTMLDDA]] Internal Slot
